candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the bearer token (any authenticated account in the realm, or a master-realm admin) and the `{member-id}` path segment, which is an arbitrary user id. No organization or realm-management role is required.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Confirmed there is no global admin-REST authorization filter: no ContainerRequestFilter/PreMatching auth filter in the admin package; AdminRoot authenticates only, and each endpoint is expected to check permissions itself. Confirmed the method has no indirect check: it passes organization=null and never touches `auth`; the delegate's getUser() only does a null check. Confirmed sibling methods in the same class (create/search/get) do call requireManageRealm, so the omission is inconsistent with the class's own policy. I could not run the server, so reachability is established from JAX-RS path/source structure only, not runtime.
candidates.impact: Authorization bypass / information disclosure: any authenticated realm user can enumerate which organizations an arbitrary user belongs to and read organization metadata (name, alias, description, enabled state, verified email domains, redirect URL). In multi-tenant/organization setups this leaks tenant membership and configuration that the admin REST API otherwise restricts to realm management.
candidates.prerequisites: Organizations feature enabled and at least one organization present; attacker holds any valid access token issued by the target realm (or by the master realm for cross-realm access). Admin REST API enabled (default).
candidates.root_cause: OrganizationsResource.getOrganizations() exposes the path `members/{member-id}/organizations` but never calls `auth.realm().requireManageRealm()` (or any other permission check), unlike create/search/get in the same class and all other organization sub-resources. It directly delegates to OrganizationMemberResource.getOrganizations(), which (with organization == null) only resolves the target user by id and returns provider.getByMember(user) with ModelToRepresentation.toRepresentation(org) (id, name, alias, enabled, redirectUrl, description, domains). No authorization check exists anywhere on this path.
candidates.title: Missing authorization on admin endpoint listing a user's organizations
candidates.trace: Request GET /admin/realms/{realm}/organizations/members/{userId}/organizations -> AdminRoot.getRealmsAdmin() only performs bearer-token authentication (AdminRoot.authenticateRealmAdminRequest, lines 169-201) and RealmsAdminResource.getRealmAdmin() only enforces same-realm/master-realm (lines 200-215) -> RealmAdminResource.organizations() returns OrganizationsResource (RealmAdminResource.java lines 622-625, also unchecked at that point) -> JAX-RS matches the literal `members` segment ahead of the `{org-id}` template, so OrganizationsResource.getOrganizations (no check) is invoked -> new OrganizationMemberResource(session, null, adminEvent).getOrganizations(member-id) -> getUser() calls session.users().getUserById(realm, id) with no permission check -> provider.getByMember(user) is streamed back as OrganizationRepresentation objects. By contrast, create/search/get in the same class call auth.realm().requireManageRealm() (lines 100, 154, 171), as do the organization member/IdP invitation endpoints via their parent.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. It is possible (though inconsistent with the rest of the class) that exposing user organization membership to any authenticated user was intended; if so this is a hardening issue rather than a vulnerability. The exact CVE/fix for the benchmarked case could not be confirmed from source alone.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-862 Missing Authorization / CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

coverage_summary: Read the raw snapshot through list/search/read tools: 5,866 model-visible files (binary files refused; no name/symlink exclusions reported). Java src/test trees are empty and .adoc/.ftl/.tsx are absent, so Java unit tests, docs and templates were not reviewable; JavaScript .ts/.json resources were only spot-checked. I inspected, in whole or relevant part: OIDC AuthorizationEndpoint/Checker/RedirectUtils/WebOriginsUtils, TokenEndpoint-adjacent grant and token-exchange providers (V1/V2), LogoutEndpoint, PAR/device/CIBA, SAML broker SAMLEndpoint/SamlService/DocumentUtil signature and destination handling, action-token handlers (execute-actions/verify-email/update-email/invite-org/idp-verify), AuthenticationManager/session-code checks, admin REST plumbing (AdminRoot, RealmsAdminResource, RealmAdminResource), Organizations admin resources, FGAP v1/v2 permission evaluators (MgmtPermissions(V2), Role/User/Group/ClientPermissions(V2), FGAPDecision/FGAPEvaluation/PartialEvaluator), LDAP query escaping, account REST resources, DefaultCors, locale handling, and assorted utilities. Most of the repository (adapters, operator, distribution, testsuite, remaining admin resources) was not read line-by-line; no runtime, build, or exploit execution was performed.
limitations: The finding is a static source lead; I did not execute the server, so reachability/authorization behavior is inferred from JAX-RS mapping and the absence of a global admin auth filter, not runtime-confirmed.
Java tests were removed from the snapshot, so I could not check expected authorization behavior or identify the benchmarked fix via tests.
No ground-truth CVE/patch metadata was consulted (per instructions); the mapping from this issue to a specific CVE is unverified.
Feature flags matter: the Organizations feature must be enabled and at least one organization must exist for the endpoint to return data.

Large parts of the monorepo (adapters, operator, distribution, federation, most other admin resources) were sampled rather than exhaustively reviewed; a higher-impact Java issue may exist in unread areas.

Whether the missing permission check is the intended behavior (a low-privilege read endpoint) or a vulnerability could not be resolved from source alone; the inconsistency with sibling methods is the main evidence.

rejected_leads.lead: InviteOrgActionTokenHandler uses token.getRedirectUri() (from organization.getRedirectUrl()) without RedirectUtils.verifyRedirectUri, unlike ExecuteActions/VerifyEmail/UpdateEmail handlers
rejected_leads.reason: Real divergence from sibling handlers, but the redirect value is embedded in a signed action token created only through the admin organization-invitation resource from an admin-configured organization redirect URL; attacker control is weak (requires organization/admin configuration) and browsers generally ignore javascript: in a 302 Location, so impact/control is too uncertain to prefer over the missing-authz candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: StandardTokenExchangeProvider.validateAudience() does not call ClientPermissions.canExchangeTo() for requested audiences (V1 AbstractTokenExchangeProvider does)
rejected_leads.reason: The `audience` parameter only adds audience entries to a token still issued for the requester, and the standard (RFC 8693) provider intentionally relies on the subject-token audience check; also ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException, so the omission looks deliberate for the V2 feature. No concrete privilege gain could be established.

Counterevidence found: V1 RolePermissions.canMapRole (line 313-315) and canMapComposite (line 403-405) contain the identical per-client shortcut without checkAdminRoles; the V2 code mirrors V1 semantics, so this is not a regression.

rejected_leads.lead: WebAuthn AttestationStatementSerializationContainer uses Jackson @JsonTypeInfo(Id.NAME) with an attacker-influenced fmt value
rejected_leads.reason: The companion AttestationStatementConverter is dead code in this snapshot (no callers; credentials store only attestationStatementFormat), and webauthn4j only produces known AttestationStatement subtypes for known formats, so the unsafe polymorphic read is not reachable here.

rejected_leads.lead: Misc: DefaultCors preflight echoes any Origin; OrganizationsResource.create/update validate redirectUrl only with a generic URI validator; various V2 permission helpers rely on hasPermission()
rejected_leads.reason: Preflight reflection does not expose data (real requests are still checked), URI validation is admin-only input, and no concrete authorization bypass could be demonstrated; kept only as rejected leads.

summary: I reviewed the assigned Keycloak (999.0.0-SNAPSHOT, ~26.2-era: Quarkus 3.20.0, jpa-changelog-26.2.0 only, JS deps from April 2025) Java server code as a defensive source review, focusing on OIDC endpoints (authorization/redirect, token, logout, PAR, device, CIBA, token exchange), SAML broker verification, admin REST authorization (incl. Organizations and the new FGAP v2 permission evaluators), action-token handlers, account REST, LDAP, CORS and cookie/redirect handling. One concrete, source-verifiable authorization omission stands out: the admin REST endpoint `GET /admin/realms/{realm}/organizations/members/{member-id}/organizations` performs no permission check at all, while every sibling method in the same class requires `auth.realm().requireManageRealm()`. Because `AdminRoot.getRealmsAdmin`/`RealmsAdminResource` only authenticate a bearer token and check same/master realm (no admin-role filter), any authenticated user of the realm can invoke it and read arbitrary users' organization membership together with organization metadata (name/alias/domains/redirect URL/description). I submitted this single candidate. Other plausible-looking spots were checked and rejected or remain unconfirmed (listed below).
